section_1.title: Prerequisites: The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
section_1.content: Briefly review the IVT: If a continuous function changes sign, it must cross zero. Visualize this as a hiker crossing a mountain range; if they start below a cloud layer and end above it, they must pass through the cloud.
section_1.example: A hiker climbing from sea level to 1000m must pass through exactly 500m elevation.

section_2.title: Problem Statement: The Inscribed Square
section_2.content: Introduce the conjecture: Can every simple closed curve (a loop that doesn't intersect itself) have four points that form the vertices of a square? Show a circle and a random 'blob' shape side-by-side.
section_2.example: Imagine a stretchy rubber band twisted into an irregular closed loop; we are searching for 4 points on that band that create a perfect square.

section_3.title: Topological Mapping: The Configuration Space
section_3.content: Explain how we map pairs of points $(x, y)$ on the curve to a 3D space. The set of all chords forms a surface. Explain that finding a square is equivalent to finding a point where the midpoint and distance conditions align.
section_3.example: Visualizing a 'map' of all possible chords on the loop, where the axes represent the position of the two points on the boundary.

section_4.title: The Solution Strategy: Parity and Symmetry
section_4.content: Demonstrate the use of the 'winding number' or the antipodal map. If we rotate the square configuration, the difference between the 'midpoint' and the 'distance' constraints must vanish at some point due to continuous deformation.
section_4.example: Using a robotic arm tracing the loop: as the arm adjusts to maintain a square, the continuous movement forces a intersection point where the 'square' property is satisfied.

section_5.title: Summary and Open Frontiers
section_5.content: Summarize that the theorem holds for all smooth curves (proven by Emch/Levien). Mention the generalization: the Inscribed Rectangle Problem (proven) vs. the Inscribed Square Problem for non-smooth curves (still an active area of research).
section_5.example: Concluding with a digital animation of a square 'locking' into place on a dynamic, morphing organic shape.
